The Chicago School: Phone Calls as Leads

Prepared Nov. 2, 2026 · CallRail data through Oct. 31, 2026

Before reading: the application rates on this page come from an old Salesforce export. The 22% vs 9% finding matches callers to the most recent Salesforce lead export Mason has, which covers leads from 2014–2017. The call data is current through October 2026; the match to applications is not. To bring it up to date, we need a new Salesforce export of leads created since October 2024: phone number, created date, lead source, and application and start flags. No names or emails are needed.

Phone calls are the one lead source that never reaches Salesforce. Mason has tracked calls from paid search since 2013, first in Marchex and since 2020 in CallRail, and has now matched a decade of callers to Salesforce leads. The pattern is clear: callers who stayed on the line 5 minutes or more applied at 22%, more than double the 9% of shorter calls. In 2026 about 95 calls a month run that long, and none of them are counted as leads or attributed to the campaign that drove them.

Call volume is flat year over year (—), but call quality has changed. In October, — of callers hung up before reaching anyone, and — of answered calls ended within a minute. Only The Chicago School's paid-search visitors are tracked; Saybrook, Pacific Oaks and Colleges of Law have no tracking numbers in CallRail.

Which calls are leads? Five minutes is the line

Callers who applied, by longest call

9,852 unique callers to Chicago School tracking numbers, 2014–2017, matched by phone number to Salesforce leads with an application received.

Why 5 minutes, not 10 or 20

  • The jump happens at 5 minutes. Application rates sit around 8–11% for calls under 5 minutes, then nearly double to 20% for 5–10 minute calls.
  • 10 minutes adds little precision. Callers at 10+ minutes applied at 25%, versus 22% at 5+ minutes.
  • But it loses half the applicants. A 5-minute line captures 477 of the 1,205 callers who applied; a 10-minute line captures 281.
  • 20+ minutes is a strong signal, not a sure one. 28% of those callers applied.
  • This is the same line Mason proposed in July 2014: count unique calls over 5 minutes as leads.

One 5-minute call, in detail

An answered call from Oct 5, 2026, 12.6 minutes long, summarized from CallRail's transcript. The caller's details are left out. Caller ID showed a government office line, a reminder that caller ID names describe the phone line, not the person calling.

  • Who called. A practicing, master's-level psychologist who had finished all coursework, internships and comprehensive exams for a doctorate elsewhere, but not the dissertation. The caller lives in Virginia, near Washington, D.C., and works full time.
  • What they wanted. The caller saw a paid ad for the Psy.D. and called about the 3-year Applied Clinical Psychology program, hoping earlier credits would transfer.
  • What they heard. The distance format is open only to residents of California, Texas and West Virginia, so the only option would be the 5-year on-campus Psy.D. Tuition was quoted at $1,879 per credit hour.
  • How it ended. The rep tried to transfer the call to admissions, but no one was available. After about four minutes on hold, the rep took a name and number for a callback "within about 10 minutes."
  • What happened next. Three days later the caller returned to the website and read the tuition and fees page. Whether admissions ever called back isn't recorded anywhere we can see, because calls don't reach Salesforce.
  • Why it matters. This is the kind of caller the 5-minute line is meant to catch: a qualified, high-intent prospect driven by paid media, who today is counted nowhere as a lead and whose follow-up can't be tracked.

A long call that wasn't a prospective student

An answered call from Oct 27, 2026, 17 minutes long, summarized from CallRail's transcript. The caller's details are left out.

  • Who called. The human resources office of a California county mental health department, after about two minutes in the hold queue.
  • What they wanted. To confirm whether two Psy.D. programs qualify job candidates for a California psychologist license.
  • What they heard. The rep confirmed from the school's licensure disclosures that the Clinical Forensic Psy.D. qualifies. A question about extra coursework California requires for the Applied Clinical Psy.D. went unanswered, and the rep took contact details for a callback.
  • Why it matters. A few 5+ minute calls come from employers or agencies, not prospective students. They aren't leads, which is another reason to match calls against a fresh Salesforce export. They still matter: an employer that hires these graduates had a licensing question no one on the phone could answer.

More than a decade of call tracking

Mason holds the only continuous record of Chicago School phone demand: Marchex call logs, a Salesforce lead export, and CallRail.

WhenWhat
2012 – Mar 2020Marchex call tracking on Chicago School ads: about 20,700 calls logged, with caller number, campaign line and duration.
2013 – 2015Monthly Inbound Phone Call Tracking Reports sent to TCS Ed System marketing (Regi Dennis, Alison Baumann and team).
Jul 2014Mason proposes defining a phone lead by call length (all calls, unique 2+ min, unique 5+ min, 20+ min) and recommends unique calls over 5 minutes.
2014 – 2017Salesforce lead export for The Chicago School shared with Mason (about 190,000 leads with home phone, application and start flags). Matching callers to it began in 2018; the results are on this page.
Feb 2020Tracking moves from Marchex to CallRail.
Apr – May 2022TCS Ed System Inbound Call Log sent to Tiffani: a review of recorded calls across The Chicago School, Pacific Oaks, Saybrook and Colleges of Law. It found long calls that were callers stuck in the phone menu (7 of 39 Chicago School calls over 10 minutes).
Oct 2024 – Oct 2026CallRail: 8,373 tracked calls, shown below.

What this data can and can't tell us

  • Matching is by phone number only. We compare the number a caller dialed from with the home phone on the Salesforce record. If someone calls from a spouse's, family or work phone, or from a number that isn't on their record, the call won't match. Every rate here is a floor.
  • Applications, not enrollments. "Started Class" is filled in for only 641 students in the export, nearly all 2014 terms, too few to measure. Enrollment data from Salesforce would finish the picture.
  • Call length includes hold and menu time. The 2022 call review found callers stuck in a menu loop for about 13 minutes. Long calls should be checked against recordings, and talk time used where available.
  • Paid search only. Tracking numbers show to paid-search visitors. Callers from organic search, email or direct visits dial the main admissions number and aren't counted.
  • Order isn't tested. A match means the caller also applied at some point, before or after the call.

What we recommend

  • Count answered calls of 5+ minutes as phone leads and send them to Salesforce with campaign, keyword and landing page, so they show up in source attribution next to form leads.
  • Match callers to Salesforce leads every month by phone number, and share starts or enrollments so we can measure call-to-enrollment directly.
  • Fix the queue and voicemail. By October, 27% of weekday business-hours calls ended in the hold queue or at voicemail, up from 11% in June. Weekend callers almost never reach a person, and the voicemail box sometimes fails outright (see the appendix).
  • Add tracking for Saybrook, Pacific Oaks and Colleges of Law; today their phone demand is invisible.
  • Add a tracking number for organic/SEO visitors, so all click-to-calls are counted, not just paid.

Appendix: what 1,485 call transcripts show

CallRail has transcribed every recorded call since May 22, 2026. We read all 1,485 (May 22 – Oct 31) to see what happens after the phone rings: whether callers reach a person, how long they wait, who answers and what they ask about. Outcomes are classified from the transcript text; times are Eastern.

More callers never reach a person

Weekday calls, 9–5 ET. Failed = caller hung up in the hold queue, or the call ended at voicemail.

Failed to reach a personWaited 60+ seconds before a person picked up

Outside business hours, almost no one gets through

All transcribed calls by time of week. Callers who gave up in the queue waited a median of 2 minutes first. In 40 calls the voicemail system itself failed ("This operation cannot be completed at this time").

WhenCallsReached a personGave up on holdVoice­mailUnclear

What callers ask about

Share of calls that reached a person in which the caller raised each topic. A call can raise several.

In callers' own words

Most frequent words and phrases from the caller side of every call that reached a person; larger means more often.

Calls by admissions rep

Rep names are taken from the greeting ("Hello, this is Wendy at the Chicago School on a recorded line"); 423 calls had no name we could pick out, and spellings come from speech recognition. Wait time mostly reflects the queue, not the rep. Talk time and the share of calls running 5+ minutes are the fairer comparison. Reps with 5 or more calls.
